questions.stem: Which memory file applies to every repository a single developer works on, on their own machine, without being shared with teammates?

options.text: `./CLAUDE.md`
`~/.claude/CLAUDE.md`
`.claude/settings.json`
The enterprise managed policy file

questions.explanation: `~/.claude/CLAUDE.md` is user-scoped memory: it loads in every project for that user and is never committed. `./CLAUDE.md` is project memory shared through git; managed policy is organisation-wide and administrator-owned.

questions.stem: A `CLAUDE.md` is growing past 500 lines and is loaded on every single turn. Which technique keeps the always-on cost down while leaving the detail available?

options.text: Move the detail into separate documents and reference them by path, so they are read only when relevant.
Compress the file by removing all whitespace and newlines.
Move everything into `settings.json`, which is not counted against context.
Split it into ten `CLAUDE.md` files in the same directory; only the first is loaded.

questions.explanation: This is progressive disclosure. Keep the always-loaded file to a short, high-signal index — build commands, hard rules, layout — and point to deeper documents (`See docs/testing.md for the test strategy`) that are pulled in only when the task touches them.

distractor_notes.B: Whitespace is a rounding error; the tokens are in the prose, and unreadable memory is worse memory.
distractor_notes.C: Settings is configuration and cannot carry project knowledge.
distractor_notes.D: Only one `CLAUDE.md` per directory is meaningful.

analogy.text: It is the README/wiki split. The README is the map everyone reads; the wiki holds the twenty pages nobody needs on a given day.

snippet.title: A lean CLAUDE.md index
snippet.code:
# Payments service

## Commands
- Test: `pnpm test`  |  Lint: `pnpm lint`  |  Types: `pnpm typecheck`

## Hard rules
- Money is `bigint` minor units. Never floats.
- Every handler goes through `withIdempotency()`.

## Deeper reading (load only when relevant)
- Ledger invariants: @docs/ledger.md
- PSP failover runbook: @docs/psp-failover.md

questions.stem: In a monorepo, `services/payments/CLAUDE.md` documents payment-specific rules. When is it loaded?

options.text: Always, at session start, alongside the root `CLAUDE.md`.
When Claude Code works with files under `services/payments/`.
Only if the root `CLAUDE.md` imports it explicitly.
Never; only the root file is supported.

questions.explanation: Subdirectory memory is loaded on demand when work touches that subtree. That is what makes monorepo memory scale: a developer in `services/search` never pays for the payments team's rules.

distractor_notes.A: Loading every subtree's memory eagerly would blow the context budget in a large monorepo.
distractor_notes.C: An explicit import works, but is not required.

analogy.text: Root `CLAUDE.md` is cluster-wide policy; a service's `CLAUDE.md` is a namespace ConfigMap that only matters when you are in that namespace.

questions.stem: Your organisation has a 40-page incident-response runbook. Engineers need Claude Code to follow it correctly during an incident, but it is irrelevant 99% of the time. What is the best structure?

options.text: Paste the runbook into the project `CLAUDE.md`.
Package it as an Agent Skill whose description matches incident scenarios, so it loads only when triggered.
Give every engineer a personal `~/.claude/CLAUDE.md` containing the runbook.
Add it as an MCP resource that the model must fetch on every turn.

questions.explanation: Skills exist for exactly this shape: large, procedural, situational knowledge. Only the name and description sit in context permanently; the body — and any bundled scripts or templates — load when the description matches what the user is doing.

distractor_notes.A: Charges 40 pages of context on every turn of every unrelated task.
distractor_notes.C: Same cost, worse — now duplicated per engineer and impossible to update centrally.
distractor_notes.D: Fetching on every turn reproduces the always-on cost with added latency.

analogy.text: It is lazy loading versus bundling everything into the initial JavaScript payload. You ship the route, not the whole app.

---

---

# Incident response

## 1. Classify severity
...

## Reference
- Escalation matrix: ./escalation.md
- Comms templates: ./templates/

questions.stem: Select the THREE items that genuinely belong in a project `CLAUDE.md`.

options.text: The exact commands to build, test and lint the project.
A non-obvious constraint, e.g. 'the `orders` table is append-only; never issue UPDATE'.
A full copy of the REST API reference documentation.
Repository conventions a newcomer would get wrong, e.g. 'integration tests live beside the module, not in `tests/`'.
The team's on-call rota for this quarter.

questions.explanation: Memory earns its permanent context cost when it carries things that are load-bearing and not discoverable by reading a couple of files: how to run things, invariants that are invisible in the code, and conventions that violate the reader's default expectations. Bulk reference material and fast-decaying facts do not qualify.

distractor_notes.C: Large, static and rarely all needed — a skill or an on-demand document.
distractor_notes.E: Changes every quarter and has no bearing on code decisions; stale memory is actively misleading.

questions.stem: Which line in a `CLAUDE.md` correctly imports another memory file?

options.text: `@docs/architecture.md`
`!include docs/architecture.md`
`{{ docs/architecture.md }}`
`import "docs/architecture.md"`

questions.explanation: `@path` is the import syntax in memory files, and imports may nest a few levels deep. The other forms are invented.

questions.stem: Six months after adoption, a team's `CLAUDE.md` says the project uses Jest, but it migrated to Vitest four months ago. Claude keeps generating Jest-shaped tests. What does this incident best illustrate?

options.text: A model limitation that a more capable model would avoid.
That memory is code: stale instructions are authoritative and will be followed, so memory needs the same review and maintenance discipline as source.
That `CLAUDE.md` should never mention specific tools.
That the team should disable memory loading entirely.

questions.explanation: The agent is behaving correctly — it trusted the instruction it was given. Memory files carry high authority precisely because they are always in context, which makes them dangerous when stale. Treat `CLAUDE.md` as a reviewed artefact: change it in the same PR that changes the thing it describes.

distractor_notes.A: No model can know the file is lying to it.
distractor_notes.C: Tool specifics are among the most valuable content — they just have to be kept true.
distractor_notes.D: Throwing away the mechanism because it was not maintained is an overcorrection.

analogy.text: This is comment rot with teeth. A stale code comment misleads a reader who may notice; a stale `CLAUDE.md` line silently steers every generated change.

questions.stem: Mid-session, a developer wants to record a durable project rule they just discovered. What is the fastest supported way?

options.text: Begin the message with `#`, and choose which memory file to save it to.
Ask Claude to remember it; it persists automatically at session end.
Run `/compact remember this rule`.
Nothing in-session; memory can only be edited in an external editor.

questions.explanation: A message starting with `#` is captured as a memory entry, and you are asked which memory file it belongs in. `/memory` opens the files for fuller editing.

distractor_notes.B: Conversation is not persisted to memory on its own; it is discarded with the session.
distractor_notes.C: `/compact` summarises the transcript; it does not write memory files.

questions.stem: An agent is asked to fix a bug in a 300-file service. Which approach spends context most effectively?

options.text: Read every file first so the agent has complete information.
Search for the symptom, read only the files on the implicated path, then widen if the hypothesis fails.
Paste the entire repository into the prompt to eliminate tool-call latency.
Disable search tools so the agent reasons purely from `CLAUDE.md`.

questions.explanation: Targeted retrieval beats exhaustive loading. Reading everything both exhausts the window and dilutes attention across hundreds of irrelevant files — the relevant three lines end up competing with 300 files of noise.

distractor_notes.A: Guarantees context exhaustion and degrades reasoning.
distractor_notes.C: Same failure with worse cost, and most repos will not fit.
distractor_notes.D: Removes the agent's ability to find the bug at all.

analogy.text: You do not read the whole codebase to fix a null-pointer exception; you follow the stack trace. Same instinct, applied to an agent's context budget.

questions.stem: A 60-repository monorepo has one 2,000-line root `CLAUDE.md`. Engineers complain about slow, unfocused responses. Select the TWO changes that best address the root cause.

options.text: Reduce the root file to organisation-wide invariants and shared commands only.
Move per-service knowledge into `CLAUDE.md` files inside each service directory.
Increase the context window by upgrading every engineer's plan.
Convert the root file to a single line pointing at Confluence.
Ask engineers to run `/compact` after every second turn.

questions.explanation: The problem is that everyone pays for everyone else's knowledge on every turn. Splitting along the axis of relevance — global truths at the root, service truths in the service directory, loaded on demand — fixes it structurally.

distractor_notes.C: Buying a bigger window to hold more irrelevant text is treating the symptom.
distractor_notes.D: Now nothing useful is loaded and the agent cannot reach the wiki.
distractor_notes.E: Compaction is a recovery tool, not an architecture.

analogy.text: You would not put every namespace's ConfigMap into a single cluster-wide mount. Scope the configuration to where it applies.

questions.stem: Which `CLAUDE.md` line is most likely to actually change the agent's behaviour?

options.text: 'Write good, clean, maintainable code.'
'Follow best practices at all times.'
'Every exported function needs a JSDoc block with @param and @returns; CI fails without it.'
'Be careful with the database.'

questions.explanation: Effective memory is specific, checkable and states the consequence. 'Good', 'clean' and 'careful' are already the model's defaults and carry no decision content — they consume context without changing any choice.

distractor_notes.D: Careful how? It cannot be acted on.

analogy.text: The same reason 'write good code' is a useless PR comment and 'this query is unindexed on `tenant_id`, add the composite index' is a useful one.

questions.stem: A long debugging session is about to auto-compact. The engineer wants the summary to retain the reproduction steps and the three hypotheses already ruled out. What should they do?

options.text: Nothing — auto-compaction always preserves the most recent turns verbatim.
Run `/compact` with an explicit instruction naming what must survive.
Run `/clear` and re-paste the important parts.
Configure a `PreCompact` hook to raise the context limit.

questions.explanation: `/compact <instruction>` steers the summary. Compacting deliberately, at a moment you choose, with a statement of what matters, is far better than letting an automatic compaction decide for you at an arbitrary point.

distractor_notes.A: Recency is not the same as importance, and reproduction steps are usually old.
distractor_notes.D: A `PreCompact` hook can add instructions, but it cannot enlarge the context window.

questions.stem: A project `CLAUDE.md` says 'use tabs'. The user's `~/.claude/CLAUDE.md` says 'use spaces'. What is the expected outcome?

options.text: The project instruction wins for work in that project; it is the more specific scope.
The user instruction wins because it was configured first.
Claude Code refuses to start until the conflict is resolved.
Both are ignored and the model uses its own default.

questions.explanation: Memory composes from broad to specific, with the more specific scope taking priority for conflicts. A repository's own convention should beat a personal preference — otherwise the repo's formatting would depend on who edited it.

distractor_notes.B: Ordering is by scope, not by configuration time.
distractor_notes.C: There is no hard failure on conflicting guidance.

questions.stem: An autonomous agent loop runs 40 iterations against a task list. By iteration 25 it starts repeating work it already completed. What is the most likely architectural cause?

options.text: The model is non-deterministic and this is unavoidable.
Completed work is held only in conversation context, which compaction eventually discards; progress needs to live in durable external state the loop re-reads each iteration.
Tool calls are being rate-limited.
The temperature setting is too low.

questions.explanation: Conversation context is volatile — it gets summarised, truncated and eventually lost. Any long-running loop needs its progress externalised: a checklist file, an issue tracker, a database row that is read at the start of every iteration and written at the end. Context is working memory, not the system of record.

distractor_notes.A: Determinism is not the issue; state durability is.
distractor_notes.C: Rate limiting causes errors and stalls, not amnesia.

analogy.text: You do not keep workflow state in a Lambda's local variables between invocations — you keep it in the state machine's execution state or DynamoDB. An agent loop needs the same separation of compute from state.

snippet.title: Externalised progress the loop re-reads each iteration
snippet.code:
# TASKS.md — source of truth, not the transcript
- [x] Extract PaymentValidator from OrderService
- [x] Add unit tests for PaymentValidator
- [ ] Migrate callers in services/checkout   <- next
- [ ] Delete the legacy validate() helper

questions.stem: A CLAUDE.md instructs the agent to read `notes/vendor-feedback.md`, a file populated from customer submissions. Why is this a security-relevant design choice?

options.text: It is not; file contents are inert.
Content from an untrusted source enters context with no boundary, so text inside it can attempt to steer the agent's actions — it must be treated as data, never instruction.
Markdown files cannot be read safely and should be converted to plain text.
It doubles token cost.

questions.explanation: Prompt injection travels through any channel that reaches the model: files, web pages, issue comments, tool output. The mitigation is architectural — label the boundary, do not grant the session tools that make injected instructions consequential, and keep confirmation gates on outward-facing or destructive actions.

distractor_notes.A: Inert to a compiler, not to a model reading it as language.
distractor_notes.C: The format is irrelevant; the provenance is what matters.
distractor_notes.D: True but trivial next to the injection surface.

analogy.text: It is SQL injection's shape: the danger is not the string, it is that the string reaches an interpreter with authority. Parameterise — or in this case, scope the tools.
